lessons.title: How Do We Use Water?
objectives: Name ways we use water every day
Know that people, animals and plants all need water
explanation: We use water all day: to drink, to cook food, to wash our hands and bodies, to clean the house, and to water plants.
Animals need water to drink, and plants drink water through their roots. Without water, nothing could live.
Water comes to us from rain, rivers, lakes and wells. It must be clean before we drink it.

vocabulary.meaning: the clear liquid all living things need

examples: We wash hands before eating.

story.title: Pala's Thirsty Friends
story.text: Pala the dolphin heard that the animals on land were thirsty because their pond was nearly dry. The rain clouds listened, and soon — splash! — the pond filled again. The deer drank, the birds bathed, the flowers lifted their heads. "Water is life," said Pala happily.

lessons.title: Be a Water Saver
objectives: Practise ways to save water
Explain why saving water matters
prerequisites: Knows we use water every day
explanation: Clean water is precious. In many places, there isn't enough, especially in summer before the monsoon.
We can save water: turn off the tap while brushing teeth, take a bucket bath instead of a long shower, and tell a grown-up about leaking taps.
We can reuse water too: water used to wash vegetables can water the plants.

vocabulary.meaning: water escaping through a small hole or crack

examples: A dripping tap can waste many litres a day.

story.text: Drip, drip, drip went the tap in Momo's house all night. In the morning, Momo put a bucket underneath and found it half full! "That much water, just wasted," Momo gasped. Momo told Papa Bear, who fixed the tap, and they used the bucket water for the garden.

lessons.title: From Mountain to Sea
objectives: Describe the journey of a river from source to mouth
Explain why people settle near rivers
explanation: A river starts at its source, often high in the mountains from melting snow, a spring or rain. Up there it is a small, fast stream rushing over rocks.
Smaller streams called tributaries join it, and it grows bigger. On flat land it flows slowly and bends in loops.
At its mouth, the river meets the sea. People have built villages and cities near rivers for thousands of years for water, fish, farming and transport.

vocabulary.meaning: a smaller river that joins a bigger one
where a river meets the sea

examples: The Ganga starts at the Gangotri Glacier.
Kolkata grew beside the Hooghly, a branch of the Ganga.

story.title: The Little Stream Who Grew
story.text: High in the mountains, a tiny stream trickled from a melting glacier. "I'm so small," it sighed. Down the hill, another stream joined it — then another, and another. By the time it reached the plains, it was a wide, gentle river, carrying boats and watering fields. At last it reached the sea and whispered, "I made it!"

lessons.title: What Lives in a Pond?
objectives: Name plants and animals that live in or near ponds
Explain how pond plants help animals
explanation: Ponds and lakes are freshwater habitats — the water isn't salty like the sea. Fish, frogs, snails, water beetles, dragonflies and ducks live there.
Water plants like the lotus and water lily float on top; their leaves give shade and shelter. Tiny green algae are food for small creatures.
Many insects, like dragonflies and mosquitoes, spend their young life underwater before flying away.

vocabulary.meaning: a small area of still water
a water plant with large floating leaves and flowers

examples: The lotus is India's national flower.
Dragonfly nymphs live underwater for months.

story.title: The Frog's Lotus Leaf
story.text: A little frog sat on a lotus leaf in the middle of a pond. Below, fish swam in the cool shade of the leaves. A dragonfly zipped past, and a heron waited quietly at the edge. "Our pond is a whole city," the frog croaked.

lessons.title: India's Great Rivers
objectives: Locate major Indian rivers on a map
Distinguish Himalayan from peninsular rivers
explanation: Himalayan rivers — the Ganga, Yamuna, Brahmaputra and Indus — are fed by snow and glaciers as well as rain, so they flow all year.

Peninsular rivers — like the Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri — depend mainly on monsoon rain, so they can become low in the dry season. Most flow east into the Bay of Bengal; the Narmada and Tapi flow west into the Arabian Sea.
Rivers are central to Indian life and culture. Many people consider rivers like the Ganga sacred, and festivals are held on their banks.

context.text: Many Hindus revere the Ganga as a sacred river and a goddess, Ganga Ma; bathing in it is believed to purify. Other rivers are also honoured in various traditions.

vocabulary.meaning: a river fed by Himalayan snow and glaciers
a river of southern India fed mainly by rain

examples: The Ganga–Brahmaputra delta (Sundarbans) is one of the largest in the world.
The Godavari is the longest river in peninsular India.

story.title: Two Rivers Meet
story.text: At Devprayag, two Himalayan rivers — the swift Bhagirathi and the Alaknanda — meet. Their waters join and from there the river is called the Ganga. Travellers stand on the bridge watching the two different-coloured streams flow together into one.

lessons.title: Why Does the Sea Come and Go?
objectives: Name the seas around India
Explain what causes waves and tides
explanation: India has the Arabian Sea to the west, the Bay of Bengal to the east and the Indian Ocean to the south. India's coastline is several thousand kilometres long.
Waves are made mostly by wind blowing across the water. Stronger winds make bigger waves.
Tides are the slow rise and fall of the sea, usually twice a day. They are caused mainly by the Moon's gravity pulling on the oceans, with help from the Sun.

vocabulary.meaning: the regular rise and fall of the sea level
when the sea comes furthest up the shore
when the sea is furthest out

examples: At low tide you can find crabs and shells in rock pools.
Fishing boats often go out with the tides.

story.title: The Disappearing Beach
story.text: In the morning, Kiko built a sandcastle near the water. After lunch, the sea had crept up and washed it away! "The sea moved!" Kiko said. "That's the tide," explained Pala. "The Moon pulls the ocean, and twice a day the water comes in and goes out."

lessons.title: From River to Tap
objectives: Describe the steps in treating water
Explain how sanitation prevents disease
explanation: River or lake water can contain mud, germs and chemicals. Water treatment plants clean it in steps: screening (removing large rubbish), sedimentation (letting mud settle), filtration (passing through sand and gravel), and disinfection (often with chlorine) to kill germs.
At home, boiling water or using a reliable purifier can make it safer to drink.

Sanitation means safe toilets and safe disposal of waste. Without it, germs from human waste can get into water and cause diseases like diarrhoea and cholera. Handwashing with soap after using the toilet and before eating is one of the most effective ways to prevent illness.

context.text: The World Health Organization identifies unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene as major causes of diarrhoeal disease, especially among young children.

examples: Clear-looking water can still contain harmful germs.
India's Swachh Bharat Mission built millions of toilets.

story.title: John Snow's Map
story.text: In London in 1854, many people fell ill with cholera. Dr John Snow marked each case on a map and noticed they clustered around one water pump on Broad Street. When the pump handle was removed, cases in the area dropped. It helped show that dirty water could spread disease.

lessons.title: Polluted Rivers
objectives: Identify sources of water pollution
Explain effects on ecosystems and people
explanation: Water pollution comes from untreated sewage, factory waste, farm fertilisers and pesticides washing off fields, and plastic litter.
Extra fertilisers can cause algal blooms: algae grow quickly, then die and decompose, using up oxygen in the water so fish suffocate. Plastics harm animals that swallow them or get tangled.
Clean-up needs many actions: treating sewage before it enters rivers, stopping industrial dumping, careful fertiliser use, reducing plastic, and community clean-ups.

vocabulary.meaning: waste water from homes and toilets
a chemical used to kill pests

examples: Microplastics have been found in rivers and seas worldwide.
Sewage treatment plants clean water before releasing it.

story.title: The River Clean-Up
story.text: A group of students in Pune noticed plastic piling up along their local river. Every Sunday for a year, they and their families picked up litter, recorded what they found, and wrote to their municipal ward about the main sources. Slowly, new bins appeared and a drain was fixed.

lessons.title: Aquifers and the Water Table
objectives: Explain how groundwater is stored and recharged
Analyse the effects of over-extraction
explanation: When rain soaks into the ground, it fills the tiny spaces between soil and rock particles. Layers of rock that hold and let water through are called aquifers. The top of this saturated zone is the water table.
Wells and borewells pump groundwater up. India is among the largest users of groundwater in the world, much of it for irrigation.
If water is pumped out faster than rain can recharge it, the water table falls. Wells must go deeper, some dry up, and in coastal areas seawater can seep in.

context.text: The Central Ground Water Board reports that groundwater is over-exploited in many blocks, especially in parts of Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu.

vocabulary.meaning: an underground layer of rock or soil that holds water
the top level of underground water
a narrow, deep well drilled to reach groundwater

examples: Old stepwells (baoris) reached groundwater by steps.
Paved cities let less rain soak in, reducing recharge.

story.title: The Deepening Well
story.text: Grandfather remembered that the village well was only 10 metres deep when he was a boy. Now the borewell went down 200 metres. "We took water faster than the rain gave it back," he said. The village began building check dams and recharge pits — and slowly, the water table started to rise.

revision.notes: Self-test, explain the reasoning aloud, connect to other subjects, and attempt a transfer problem.

lessons.title: Catch the Rain
objectives: Describe modern and traditional rainwater harvesting
Calculate the rainwater a roof can collect
explanation: Rainwater harvesting means collecting rain where it falls and storing it or letting it soak into the ground. Rooftop systems channel rain through pipes into tanks or recharge pits.

India has many traditional systems: johads (earthen check dams) in Rajasthan, kunds (covered underground tanks) in desert areas, stepwells in Gujarat and Rajasthan, and eris (tank systems) in Tamil Nadu.
Harvest potential: roof area (m²) × rainfall (m) × collection efficiency. A 100 m² roof with 0.8 m of rain a year at 80% efficiency could collect about 64,000 litres.

context.text: Communities in Alwar district, Rajasthan, working with the organisation Tarun Bharat Sangh from the 1980s, revived johads, and several seasonal rivers were reported to flow again.

vocabulary.meaning: a pit that lets water soak into the ground

examples: Chennai made rooftop rainwater harvesting mandatory for buildings in the early 2000s.
Stepwells like Rani ki Vav are UNESCO World Heritage sites.

story.title: The River That Came Back
story.text: In a dry district of Rajasthan, villagers rebuilt old earthen johads to catch monsoon rain. Year after year, more water soaked into the ground. Wells refilled. Then one season, a river that had been dry for decades began to flow again. "We didn't make rain," an elder said. "We just learned to hold it."

lessons.title: Who Gets the River?
objectives: Analyse a river-sharing dispute from multiple perspectives
Evaluate mechanisms for resolving water conflicts
explanation: When rivers flow through several states or countries, sharing water fairly is difficult — especially in dry years. Upstream users can affect downstream users.

In India, the Kaveri water dispute between Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Puducherry has lasted over a century; tribunals and the Supreme Court have issued allocations, and a management authority now oversees sharing.

Internationally, the Indus Waters Treaty (1960) between India and Pakistan, brokered by the World Bank, allocated the eastern rivers mainly to India and the western rivers mainly to Pakistan. Such agreements show cooperation is possible, though they face strains.

context.text: Each party in a water dispute frames fairness differently — by historical use, population, area, or need. Analysing a dispute requires understanding these competing principles.

vocabulary.meaning: a body set up to judge a specific dispute

examples: Drought years intensify Kaveri tensions.
The Mekong River is shared by six countries.

story.title: The Farmer and the City
story.text: Upstream, a farmer needed water for sugarcane. Downstream, a city needed drinking water and farmers needed water for rice. In a dry year there wasn't enough for all. The students role-playing the dispute realised: every side had a real need. Fairness required data, compromise and trust.

lessons.title: The Ocean's Role in Climate
objectives: Explain how oceans regulate climate
Analyse threats from warming and acidification
explanation: Oceans absorb enormous amounts of heat and carbon dioxide. Currents move warm and cold water around the globe, shaping regional climates and the monsoon.
Because oceans absorb CO₂, seawater is becoming more acidic. Ocean acidification makes it harder for corals and shellfish to build shells and skeletons.

Warming oceans expand, and melting land ice adds water, so sea levels rise. Coastal cities and low-lying areas, including parts of India's coastline and the Sundarbans, face increased flooding and erosion risks.

context.text: The IPCC reports that the ocean has absorbed over 90% of the excess heat from human-caused warming and around a quarter to a third of human CO₂ emissions.

vocabulary.meaning: a large, continuous movement of seawater
corals losing their algae under stress

examples: Coral bleaching events have affected reefs including in Lakshadweep.
Mangroves can help coasts adapt to rising seas.

story.title: The Fading Reef
story.text: A diver returned to a reef she had visited ten years earlier. Where there had been brilliant colours, many corals were pale and white — bleached by a marine heatwave. In some patches, young corals were growing again. "Reefs can recover," she wrote, "if we give them a chance."
